steps: Decompose the space into generalized eigenspaces of A. Put S=+I on those with positive real part, and S=-I on the others. This is basis-independent and gives the three identities.

For uniqueness, a commuting involution T is diagonalizable with eigenvalues ±1. Its ±1 eigenspaces are A-invariant. Positive stability of TA forces the spectrum of each restriction of A into the matching half-plane; every generalized eigenspace of A therefore lies in the corresponding eigenspace of T.
The two projector identities follow by expanding S²=I. For real A, conjugation preserves the half-plane decomposition, so S and the projectors are real.
For Re(z)≠0, Re(z+1/z) has the same sign as Re(z). Rational spectral mapping therefore keeps each iterate away from the imaginary axis, preserving its sign and invertibility.
Each iterate commutes with S. Expanding (Xk±S)² yields X(k+1)±S=(1/2)Xk⁻¹(Xk±S)². Dividing these commuting factors gives G(k+1)=Gk².

The eigenvalues of G are (λ-sign(λ))/(λ+sign(λ)), all strictly within the unit disk. Matrix-power convergence gives G^(2^k)→0, and continuity of inversion at I proves convergence. The exact error identity gives the quadratic norm estimate.
The spectra of A and -B are disjoint, so the Sylvester equation has a unique solution.
For M=[[A,C],[0,-B]] and T=[[I,2X],[0,-I]], T²=I. The off-diagonal blocks of MT and TM agree exactly when AX+XB=C.
MT is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks A and B, hence is positive stable. The uniqueness characterization of the matrix sign gives T=sign(M).
Expand I-AXk(2I-AXk)=(I-AXk)² without commuting A and Xk. Induction gives Ek=E0^(2^k).
The spectral-radius hypothesis excludes 1 from spec(E0), so AX0=I-E0 is invertible. Finite-dimensional determinant multiplicativity gives invertibility of A.
Xk-A⁻¹=-A⁻¹Ek. Matrix-power convergence proves the limit, and submultiplicativity gives the explicit bound when ||E0||2=q<1.
Write a thin SVD A=U diag(si) V*. If Xk=U diag(si,k) V*, its pseudoinverse adjoint is U diag(1/si,k) V*. Positivity is preserved and si,k+1=(si,k+1/si,k)/2.
For c(s)=(s-1)/(s+1), c((s+1/s)/2)=c(s)². Thus si,k=(1+ci^(2^k))/(1-ci^(2^k)). This indexes diagonal entries in the fixed singular-vector basis, with no claim that their order is preserved.
The polar factor is UV*. Taking the maximum of |si,k-1| gives the bound with r=max|ci|. All denominators are positive.
In a fixed thin SVD the map is f(s)=s(3-s²)/2. For 0<s<sqrt(3), f(s)>0 and f(s)≤1, with maximum 1 at s=1. Thus the first iterate has all singular values in (0,1].
Since Xnew=X(I+E/2) and X*X=I-E, expand I-(I+E/2)(I-E)(I+E/2)=(3/4)E²+(1/4)E³.
For k≥1, the eigenvalues of E lie in [0,1), so delta(k+1)≤(3+delta(k))delta(k)²/4≤delta(k)². Finally 1-s≤1-s² for 0<s≤1 bounds the polar error by the defect.

For Hermitian X, ||A-X||F²=||H-X||F²+||K||F². In an eigenbasis of H, write Y=U*XU. Feasibility implies yii≥delta, and ||diag(lambda)-Y||F² is the sum of squared diagonal errors plus nonnegative squared off-diagonal entries.

Each diagonal term is uniquely minimized at max(lambda_i,delta); every off-diagonal entry must vanish to attain the minimum. The resulting diagonal matrix is feasible, proving existence, uniqueness and the distance formula.
For projections P=Pdelta(A), Q=Pdelta(B), differentiating along feasible segments gives <A-P,Q-P>R≤0 and <B-Q,P-Q>R≤0. Adding yields ||P-Q||F²≤<P-Q,A-B>R≤||P-Q||F||A-B||F.
For any admissible perturbation E and a unit eigenvector v of A+E, (zI-A)v=Ev, so sigma_min(zI-A)≤||E||2.
Choose a unit right singular vector v attaining the minimum, and set w=(zI-A)v and E=wv*. Then Ev=w, (A+E)v=zv, rank(E)≤1, and ||E||2=||w||2=sigma_min. If w=0, E=0 handles the eigenvalue case.
Away from the spectrum, the inverse singular values are reciprocals and its norm is 1/sigma_min. For a normal matrix, unitary diagonalization gives sigma_min(zI-A)=min_lambda|z-lambda|.
For u(t)=exp(tA)v, differentiate ||u(t)||² to obtain 2 Re<u,Au>=2<u,Hu>≤2 omega||u||². Multiplication by exp(-2 omega t) shows monotonicity and yields the norm bound.
If ||exp(tA)||≤exp(ct) for every t≥0, apply to any unit v, square and differentiate at t=0 from the right: 2<v,Hv>≤2c. Taking the maximal Rayleigh quotient gives omega≤c.
The equivalence with contractivity follows by setting c=0 and using the Hermitian norm/order correspondence. The exponent may be negative.

proof: Let $G=A^*A+L^*L$. For each vector $z$, $z^*Gz=\|Az\|_2^2+\|Lz\|_2^2$, hence $G\succeq0$ and $\ker G=\ker A\cap\ker L$. In particular $\operatorname{rank}G=q$.

Choose a unitary (orthogonal over R) $V$ with $V^*GV=\operatorname{diag}(g_1,\ldots,g_q,0,\ldots,0)$, where $g_i>0$. Let $T=V\operatorname{diag}(g_1^{-1/2},\ldots,g_q^{-1/2},1,\ldots,1)$. This is invertible and $T^*GT=\operatorname{diag}(I_q,0)$.

Write $T=[T_1,T_0]$. Since the columns of $T_0$ lie in $\ker G$, $AT_0=LT_0=0$. On the active block, $H=T_1^*A^*AT_1$ satisfies $0\preceq H\preceq I_q$ and $T_1^*L^*LT_1=I_q-H$. Diagonalize $H$ by a unitary $U$: $U^*HU=\operatorname{diag}(h_i)$ with $0\le h_i\le1$.

Take $X=T\operatorname{diag}(U,I_{n-q})$, $c_i=\sqrt{h_i}$ and $s_i=\sqrt{1-h_i}$ on the active block, and zero elsewhere. The two Gram identities follow. Their off-diagonal entries show orthogonality of the images, and their diagonal entries give the normalization. Invertibility of X identifies the common-kernel basis.
edge_cases: q=0 gives A=L=0 and any invertible X; n=0 is vacuous.
Do not divide by c_i or s_i when it is zero. Completion to full left unitary factors is optional and uses the existing orthonormal-completion interface.

proof: The objective is the squared residual of the stacked system $[A;\sqrt\beta L]x=[b;0]$. Its normal equation is $H_\beta x=A^*b$. Positivity gives $\ker H_\beta=\ker A\cap\ker L=:K$. Since $A^*b$ is orthogonal to K, it lies in $\operatorname{range}H_\beta$; all solutions are $H_\beta^\dagger A^*b+K$.

If K=0, the normalized GSVD has q=n and $X^*H_\beta X=D_\beta=\operatorname{diag}(c_i^2+\beta s_i^2)\succ0$. Therefore $H_\beta^{-1}=X D_\beta^{-1}X^*$, proving the formula. Put $x=Xz$. The objective becomes $\|b\|^2+\sum_i[(c_i^2+\beta s_i^2)|z_i|^2-2\operatorname{Re}(\overline{z_i}(Ax_i)^*b)]$.

For $c_i>0$, the unique coordinate is $z_i(\beta)=c_i u_i^*b/(c_i^2+\beta s_i^2)$; for $c_i=0$ it is zero, because then $s_i=1$. As beta decreases to zero the former coordinates tend to $u_i^*b/c_i$. These are exactly the coordinates fixed by least squares; the free coordinates have c_i=0 and the penalty is minimized uniquely by setting them to zero.

As beta tends to infinity, coordinates with s_i>0 tend to zero. Coordinates with s_i=0 have c_i=1 and stay equal to $u_i^*b$. The condition Lx=0 is exactly z_i=0 on s_i>0, so the limit is the unique constrained least-squares solution. Uniqueness also follows because A is injective on ker L.
edge_cases: L=0 is allowed only with full-column-rank A for uniqueness and limits; then x_beta is constant.
A=0 with injective L gives x_beta=0 for every beta>0.
With a nontrivial common kernel there are infinitely many minimizers; the GSVD particular minimizer need not be the Euclidean minimum-norm one.

proof: Fix x and set $z=(x,-1)^T$. Feasibility is $(C+\Delta)z=0$ with $\Delta=[E\ f]$. Every feasible correction can be written $\Delta=-Czz^*/\|z\|^2+N$, where Nz=0. The two terms are Frobenius-orthogonal: their inner product is a scalar multiple of $\operatorname{tr}(z(Cz)^*N)=(Cz)^*Nz=0$. Thus the unique least-norm correction at fixed x is the first term, with squared norm $\|Cz\|^2/\|z\|^2$.

Every projective direction with a nonzero last coordinate has a representative (x,-1). Such directions are dense in the unit sphere. The Rayleigh quotient is continuous and has minimum mu on the full sphere, hence its infimum over feasible directions is mu. Equality holds exactly on the minimum eigenspace. This proves both attainment and the complete parametrization of optimal x.

Write the eigenvector as $v=(y,t)$ with t nonzero. If $a=\lambda_{\min}(A^*A)>\mu$, interlacing implies the second smallest eigenvalue of C*C is at least a; hence mu is simple. A minimizing vector cannot have t=0, since that would give $A^*Ay=\mu y$ with y nonzero. Therefore there is exactly one projective solution.
The first block of $C^*Cv=\mu v$ is $(A^*A-\mu I)y=-A^*bt$. Dividing by -t yields the inverse formula. For unit v, the fixed-direction correction above equals -Cvv*, so its squared norm is mu.
edge_cases: No m>=n assumption is needed for the infimum/attainment statement; use the full Gram spectrum to include rectangular domain zeros.
Example of nonattainment: A=(0,1)^T, b=(2,0)^T gives mu=1 and minimum eigenspace span((1,0)^T). The residual quotient is (x^2+4)/(x^2+1)>1 for every finite real x, approaching 1 as |x| grows.
mu=0 is allowed; whenever the direction is feasible the optimal correction is zero.

proof: First assume the pencil is regular. Choose a scalar zeta with $M=A-\zeta B$ nonsingular; such a scalar exists because the determinant polynomial is nonzero. Apply Schur triangularization to $M^{-1}B$: choose unitary Z with $H=Z^*M^{-1}BZ$ upper triangular. Then $BZ=MZH$.

Take a square QR factorization $MZ=QR$. Since MZ is invertible, Q is unitary and R is upper triangular with every diagonal entry nonzero. Thus $Q^*BZ=RH=:T$ and $Q^*AZ=R+\zeta RH=R(I+\zeta H)=:S$, both upper triangular. For each i, $t_{ii}=r_{ii}h_{ii}$ and $s_{ii}=r_{ii}(1+\zeta h_{ii})$ cannot both vanish.

For an arbitrary pair, choose nonzero epsilon_j tending to zero and avoiding the finitely many roots of det(A+epsilon I). Each pair (A+epsilon_j I,B) is regular because its determinant at lambda=0 is nonzero. The preceding construction gives unitary Q_j,Z_j. Compactness of the two unitary groups gives a jointly convergent subsequence. Its limits Q,Z remain unitary, and upper triangularity is closed, so both limiting transformed matrices are upper triangular.

Finally $A=QSZ^*$ and $B=QTZ^*$, giving the homogeneous determinant identity. For a regular pencil it is a nonzero product of n linear homogeneous factors. The vanishing direction of factor i is $[\alpha:\beta]=[s_{ii}:t_{ii}]$, including beta=0 for infinity.
edge_cases: n=0 gives the empty identity decomposition and no generalized eigenvalues.
B=0 and A nonsingular has n eigenvalues at infinity; no inverse of B is used.
For a singular pencil a zero diagonal pair occurs in any simultaneous triangularization, and the homogeneous determinant is identically zero.

proof: Since B has full row rank, $BB^*\succ0$, every constraint is feasible, and every feasible x has the unique form $x_p+Zy$. Moreover $(\ker B)^\perp=\operatorname{range}B^*$, so $\ker Z^*=\operatorname{range}B^*$.

For a homogeneous KKT solution, Bx=0 implies x=Zy, and multiplying $Hx+B^*\lambda=0$ by Z* gives $Z^*HZy=0$. If the reduced Hessian is nonsingular, y=0 and then B*lambda=0; injectivity of B* gives lambda=0. Conversely, if the reduced Hessian is singular, choose y nonzero with $Z^*HZy=0$. Then x=Zy is nonzero and $Hx\in\ker Z^*=\operatorname{range}B^*$. A multiplier lambda exists with $Hx+B^*\lambda=0$, proving singularity of K.

For nonzero f,g, substitute x=x_p+Zy into the first block and multiply by Z*. This gives the stated reduced equation. Its solution makes f-Hx orthogonal to ker B, hence in range B*. Multiplying $B^*\lambda=f-Hx$ by B gives the multiplier formula.

Substitution into the constrained quadratic gives a constant plus $\tfrac12 y^*(Z^*HZ)y-\operatorname{Re}(y^*Z^*(f-Hx_p))$. A positive definite reduced Hessian makes this quadratic strictly convex and its critical point is the unique global minimizer. Conversely, if the Hermitian reduced Hessian has a negative eigenvalue, the zero-linear-term objective is unbounded below in that direction; if it has a zero eigenvalue and no negative eigenvalues, that same objective has nonunique minima. Thus unique minimization for every f,g forces positive definiteness.
edge_cases: m=n gives an empty reduced problem; the constraint fixes x uniquely and the KKT matrix is invertible for every Hermitian H. Empty-dimensional invertibility/positive definiteness is understood in the usual vacuous sense.
m=0 reduces to the unconstrained Hessian system.
Rank-deficient B requires a different multiplier-uniqueness statement and is deliberately not hidden in these hypotheses.
solvers.reuse: Connects finite matrix analysis to constrained least squares, quadratic optimization, and saddle-point solvers without an unnecessary ambient SPD assumption.

proof: Since B* is injective and A^{-1} is positive definite, $y^*Sy=(B^*y)^*A^{-1}(B^*y)>0$ for every y nonzero. The symmetrically preconditioned matrix is $M=\begin{bmatrix}I&F^*\\F&0\end{bmatrix}$ with $F=\widehat S^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}$. F has full row rank and $FF^*=\widehat S^{-1/2}S\widehat S^{-1/2}$.

Use an SVD of F. The n-m right-nullspace directions give eigenvalue 1. Each positive singular value sqrt(mu_i) produces a two-dimensional invariant block $\begin{bmatrix}1&\sqrt{\mu_i}\\\sqrt{\mu_i}&0\end{bmatrix}$, whose characteristic equation is lambda^2-lambda-mu_i=0. This gives the complete spectrum, including multiplicities. Congruence of $c\widehat S\preceq S\preceq C\widehat S$ gives c<=mu_i<=C; monotonicity of the two scalar roots gives the stated intervals.

When Shat=S, every mu_i=1, so $(M-I)(M^2-M-I)=0$. This polynomial has value 1 at zero, so it is an admissible residual polynomial of degree three. Krylov residual minimization therefore gives zero residual in at most three steps (or earlier if some eigenvalues are absent or the initial residual has fewer spectral components).

Block elimination gives $T^{-1}K=\begin{bmatrix}I&A^{-1}B^*\\0&I\end{bmatrix}$. Its difference from I squares to zero. The polynomial (1-z)^2 equals 1 at zero and annihilates the left-preconditioned matrix, so GMRES has zero residual within two steps for every right-hand side and initial guess.
edge_cases: If n=m, eigenvalue 1 is absent from the diagonal-preconditioned spectrum, so at most two MINRES steps suffice.
The excluded m=0 case is simply the identity-preconditioned A problem.
Repeated Schur eigenvalues and repeated singular values require no special choices; the SVD block argument handles their multiplicities.
solvers.reuse: Makes Schur-complement quality an explicit spectral guarantee and supplies concrete exact preconditioner baselines for iterative-solver analysis.

proof: For Hurwitz A, a Jordan form shows $\|e^{tA}\|_2\le M(1+t^{n-1})e^{-\gamma t}$ for some M,gamma>0: each Jordan-block exponential is an exponential times a polynomial, and gamma can be chosen below minus the largest eigenvalue real part. Therefore the displayed matrix integral converges absolutely. Its integrand is Hermitian PSD. If Q is PD, continuity and the positive value $v^*Qv$ at t=0 show $v^*Xv>0$ for every v nonzero.

Differentiate $e^{tA}Qe^{tA^*}$ and integrate from 0 to infinity. The endpoint at infinity vanishes by exponential decay, giving AX+XA*=-Q. Uniqueness follows from the existing Sylvester theorem: write the operator as AX-X(-A*), and the spectra of A and -A* lie in disjoint open half-planes.

For the converse, suppose X is PD and AX+XA* is negative definite. For any eigenpair A*v=lambda v over C, $v^*(AX+XA^*)v=2\operatorname{Re}(\lambda)v^*Xv<0$. Thus every eigenvalue of A* and hence A has negative real part. The forward implication follows by taking Q=I in the integral construction.

For Q=BB*, $v^*Xv=\int_0^\infty\|B^*e^{tA^*}v\|^2dt$. This is zero iff the continuous nonnegative integrand is identically zero, which implies $B^*(A^*)^jv=0$ for all j by differentiation at zero. Conversely, the first n such equations imply every higher one by Cayley-Hamilton, and the exponential series gives $B^*e^{tA^*}v=0$. Since X is PSD, v*Xv=0 is equivalent to Xv=0. The displayed finite conditions say that v lies in the kernel of the adjoint of [B,AB,...,A^{n-1}B], yielding the rank equality.
edge_cases: B=0 gives X=0 and a zero block reachability matrix.
A Hurwitz with Q semidefinite can have singular X; strict positivity follows exactly when the finite block matrix has full row rank.
The real case is interpreted through complex eigenvectors for the converse, while the real integral solution remains real.
solvers.reuse: Supplies stability and positivity infrastructure for Lyapunov solvers, low-rank approximations, and finite-matrix Gramians.

proof: Use column-major vectorization. It is an isometry from the Frobenius matrix norm to the Euclidean vector norm and satisfies $\operatorname{vec}(AZ-ZB)=(I_n\otimes A-B^T\otimes I_m)\operatorname{vec}(Z)$. The minimum over the compact unit sphere is the least singular value of this square matrix. It is positive exactly when the operator is invertible, which is equivalent to disjoint spectra by the existing Sylvester theorem.

Let $\mathcal L(Z)=AZ-ZB$. Its least-singular-value characterization gives $\|\mathcal L Z\|_F\ge\delta\|Z\|_F$ for every Z and $\|\mathcal L^{-1}\|_{F\to F}=1/\delta$. Since R=L(X-Y), the error bound follows. A least right singular vector, reshaped as a matrix E, attains equality with residual L(E), proving sharpness.

The operator perturbation is $\mathcal D(Z)=\Delta A Z-Z\Delta B$. Mixed norm inequalities give $\|\mathcal D Z\|_F\le d\|Z\|_F$. Hence $\|(\mathcal L+\mathcal D)Z\|_F\ge(\delta-d)\|Z\|_F$. In finite equal dimensions this lower bound gives invertibility and inverse norm at most 1/(delta-d). Subtracting equations yields $(\mathcal L+\mathcal D)(\widehat X-X)=\Delta C-\Delta A X+X\Delta B$, and taking norms gives the formula.

If A and B are normal, unitary diagonalizations A=U diag(lambda)U*, B=V diag(mu)V* transform Z to U*ZV without changing its Frobenius norm. The operator acts entrywise by multiplication with lambda_i-mu_j, so its smallest singular value is the smallest modulus of those differences.
edge_cases: The m,n>=1 hypothesis avoids defining a minimum over an empty unit sphere; zero-dimensional equations are trivial and can be handled separately.
The inequality d<delta is strict; invertibility can fail at equality.
Nonnormal counterexample: A=[[1,M],[0,1]], B=[0] has spectral distance 1 but sep_F(A,B)=sigma_min(A), which tends to zero as |M| tends to infinity.
solvers.reuse: Turns small residuals into justified forward-error claims for Sylvester, Lyapunov, and projected matrix-equation solvers.

proof: Subtract the first half-step from the exact equation rearranged with beta_j to obtain $E_{j-1/2}=(A-\beta_jI)^{-1}E_{j-1}(B-\beta_jI)$. Subtract the second half-step from the corresponding exact identity to obtain $E_j=(A-\alpha_jI)E_{j-1/2}(B-\alpha_jI)^{-1}$.

Every factor involving A is a rational function of A and commutes with every other such factor, because polynomials in A commute and commuting invertible matrices have commuting inverses. The same applies to B. Induction therefore yields E_j=F_j E_0 G_j. Since R_j=A E_j-E_jB and A commutes with F_j while B commutes with G_j, the residual identity follows.

The first half-step also gives $X_{j-1/2}-X_{j-1}=(A-\beta_jI)^{-1}R_{j-1}$. Substitute this into the second step and subtract $X_{j-1}(B-\alpha_jI)$. The result is $(X_j-X_{j-1})(B-\alpha_jI)=[(A-\alpha_jI)(A-\beta_jI)^{-1}-I]R_{j-1}$, proving the stated update.

For X_0=0, R_0=C and the residual formula gives rank R_j<=rank C<=nu. Each update is a left and right multiple of the residual, so its rank is at most nu; subadditivity gives rank X_j<=j nu. Mixed norm inequalities give the error bound. Normal-matrix unitary diagonalization gives the exact spectral norm of each rational factor, including the case of vanishing numerators.
edge_cases: If alpha_j=beta_j, all factors are identity and the update is zero; the same identities remain valid.
If C=0 and X_0=0, every iterate is zero.

If the Sylvester spectra overlap, multiple exact solutions can exist; the error identity is valid relative to any chosen exact solution, but unique-solution and convergence claims need additional hypotheses.
solvers.reuse: Bridges the existing abstract displacement/Zolotarev picture to a concrete shifted-solve algorithm, its residual, and its rank growth.

proof: Let W=W_{j-1}, p=p_j, and V=V_j. The solved equation gives AV=W+pV. If the old residual is WW*, the new residual is $WW^*+2p(AVV^*+VV^*A^*)=WW^*+2p(WV^*+VW^*)+4p^2VV^*=(W+2pV)(W+2pV)^*$. Since the initial residual is BB*, induction proves the factor identity.

The residual update is $W_j=[I+2p_j(A-p_jI)^{-1}]W_{j-1}=(A+p_jI)(A-p_jI)^{-1}W_{j-1}$. Rational factors commute, so W_j=F_j B. The error E_j=X-X_j satisfies $AE_j+E_jA^*=-W_jW_j^*$. The matrix F_j X F_j* satisfies the same equation because F_j commutes with A. Lyapunov uniqueness therefore gives E_j=F_j X F_j*.

Every update 2p_j V_j V_j* is PSD, and E_j is PSD because X is. Hence the stated Loewner inequalities hold. Concatenating the scaled V_j gives Z_j. Each W_j is a left multiple of B and each V_j is a left multiple of W_{j-1}; therefore rank V_j<=rank B and rank X_j<=j rank B. The nonzero eigenvalues of W_jW_j* and W_j*W_j agree, giving both residual-norm formulas.

For one fixed p>0, $F_j=C_p^j$ with $C_p=(A+pI)(A-pI)^{-1}$. Rational spectral mapping gives eigenvalues (lambda+p)/(lambda-p), whose moduli are strictly less than one because Re(lambda)<0. Thus rho(C_p)<1, and the existing matrix-power theorem gives C_p^j->0 even for nonnormal A. The error identity proves convergence.
edge_cases: B=0 gives every iterate and residual equal to zero.
A numerator A+pI may be singular; this is harmless and can make a component exact in one step.

Counterexample to convergence for arbitrary positive shifts: for scalar A=-1 and B=1, choose p_j=2^(-j-2). Then the factors |(1-p_j)/(1+p_j)| have a strictly positive infinite product, because their deficits are summable, so the error does not tend to zero.
solvers.reuse: Provides the actual low-rank algorithm and its cheap residual evaluation, beyond a theorem that merely assumes a low-rank approximate solution.

proof: Substitute AV=VH+UT, its adjoint, and B=VB_k into the full residual. The V-by-V term is $V(HY+YH^*+B_kB_k^*)V^*$ and vanishes. The two remaining terms are exactly UTYV* and VYT*U*.

Complete [V U] to a unitary basis. In this basis, the only nonzero block of the Hermitian residual is $\begin{bmatrix}0&(TY)^*\\TY&0\end{bmatrix}$. An SVD of TY decomposes this block into pairs of eigenvalues +sigma_i and -sigma_i, plus zeros. Thus the spectral norm is ||TY||_2, the squared Frobenius norm is twice ||TY||_F^2, and the rank is twice rank(TY).

Strict dissipativity is preserved by compression: $(H+H^*)/2=V^*(A+A^*)V/2\preceq-aI$. Applying the scalar eigenvector Rayleigh quotient shows A and H are Hurwitz. The continuous Lyapunov theorem therefore gives unique PSD solutions X and Y.

For E=X-Xhat, $AE+EA^*=-R$. The integral representation, valid by linearity also for indefinite Hermitian R, gives $E=\int_0^\infty e^{tA}Re^{tA^*}dt$. The parent's logarithmic-norm theorem gives ||e^{tA}||_2<=exp(-at). For either spectral or Frobenius norm, the integrand norm is at most exp(-2at)||R||; integration gives ||E||<=||R||/(2a). Substitute the two exact residual norms.
edge_cases: ell=0 means the trial space is invariant and, when it contains B, the projected solution has zero residual and is exact if the full equation is uniquely solvable.
A stable-projection counterexample is A=[[-1,4],[0,-1]] with V=(1,1)^T/sqrt(2): A is Hurwitz but V*AV=1.
No positivity of the residual is assumed; projected residuals generally have positive and negative eigenvalues.
solvers.reuse: A practical stopping and verification theorem for polynomial, extended, or rational Krylov methods once their basis recurrence is known.

proof: For rho(A)<1, Jordan form gives constants M>0 and r<1 with ||A^j||_2<=M r^j after absorbing polynomial factors into a slightly larger r. Thus the series is absolutely convergent in either matrix norm. Each summand is PSD. Shifting the series index gives X-AXA*=Q. If a homogeneous solution D satisfies D=ADA*, then D=A^N D(A*)^N for every N; the matrix-power theorem implies the right side tends to zero, so D=0 and the solution is unique.

Split the series after N terms and factor A^N and (A*)^N out of the tail to obtain X-X_N=A^N X(A*)^N. The residual identity follows by telescoping the finite sum. In particular X_N<=X_{N+1}<=X, and rank X_N<=N rank Q.

By induction A_k=A^{2^k}. If G_k is the sum for j=0,...,2^k-1, then A_k G_k A_k* is the sum for j=2^k,...,2^{k+1}-1. Hence G_{k+1}=X_{2^{k+1}}, with base G_0=Q=X_1. This proves the exact realization, monotonicity and convergence. If Q=BB*, the proposed factor concatenation follows by multiplication.

If ||A||_2<=q<1, mixed norm inequalities bound each tail term by q^{2j}||Q||. Summing from N gives the displayed geometric estimate. For G_k this is q^{2^{k+1}}||Q||/(1-q^2). The case q=0 is interpreted directly: A=0 and every X_N with N>=1 is exact.
If rho(A)<1, take Q=I to obtain X>=I>0 with X-AXA*=I. Conversely, if X>0 and X-AXA*>0, take A*v=lambda v. Then $v^*(X-AXA^*)v=(1-|\lambda|^2)v^*Xv>0$, so every eigenvalue has modulus below one.
edge_cases: N=0 gives X_0=0 and the exact tail X; at q=0 interpret q^0=1 or use the direct A=0 statement.
Q=0 gives X=0 and zero doubling iterates.
Existence of only semidefinite X,Q does not imply rho(A)<1.
solvers.reuse: Completes the continuous/discrete matrix-equation toolkit and supplies a concrete doubling process instead of only an abstract fixed-point convergence condition.

randnla.checked_derivation: For Gram matrices G_S, determinant-zero sets are null events but adj(G_S) can be nonzero when rank=d−1. This is why unbiased pseudoinverse sums remain exact (adj(G_S)X_S*=0), while inverse-Gram sums can lose PSD adjugate contributions and become inequalities. General-position assumptions must never be dropped merely because singular subsets have probability zero.
randnla.counterexample: n=2,d=s=1, X=[1;0]. The only sample is {1}. E(G_S^-1)=1<2=(n-d+1)/(s-d+1)*(X*X)^-1. With y=[0;1], E loss=1<2=(d+1)*optimal loss.

randnla.checked_derivation: For Q*Q=I_k, after t distinct supported pivots the residual is (I−Π_t)Q*, hence its squared Frobenius norm is k−t. Product of selected squared residual norms is |det Q_S|². The k normalization factors multiply to k!, and summing k! orders gives the exact unordered projection-DPP law. This does not hold for generic RPQR input with nonconstant singular values.

For Ω=[Ω1;Ω2] Haar n-by-ell, Ω1 is r-by-ell. Let Z=(Ω1*)^+Ω2*. Bottom-unitary invariance makes E(Z*Z)=c I_(n−r). Since Ω*Ω=I, ||Z||_F²=tr((Ω1Ω1*)^-1)−r. The inverse-Beta identity yields E||Z||_F²=r(n−ell)/(ell−r−alpha), so c=r(n−ell)/[(n−r)(ell−r−alpha)]. Sign symmetry and finite second moments yield EZ=0.

Let h=κ_F²≥1,q=1−1/h, e_t=x_t−x*. For r≤s, E<e_r,e_s>=E<e_r,H^(s−r)e_r>≤q^s E0+q^(s−r)nu². On the averaging square b≤r,s<b+N, Σq^|s−r|≤N(2h−1). Also Σq^max(r,s)≤h q^b(2h−1) and ≤N²q^b. The resulting two upper bounds cover both growing and fixed burn-in. For q=0 use 0^0=1.

The source determinant proof divides by tau_r and therefore directly covers tau_r>0. At tau_r=0 and k≥r, exact-rank termination gives T_k=0 almost surely. Then Pr(T_k>0)=0, while Pr(T_k≥0)=1; an unconditional >= formulation is false. The draft uses strict > for all inputs and keeps >= only as a positive-tail variant.

matrix.scope: Algebraic reconstruction, with a corrected source formula
steps: Upper triangular block multiplication gives the ordered polynomial sums. Inverting a block upper triangular matrix gives diagonal inverses, first block -A^-1 H B^-1 and second block A^-1 G B^-1 H C^-1. Products and these inverse formulas extend the rules to P(M)Q(M)^-1.

Similarity by [[I,I],[0,I]] turns diag(A,B) into [[A,B-A],[0,B]], giving the first exact finite-difference rule with the sign adjusted. Alternatively the polynomial rule telescopes and inversion preserves it.
Varying the second base argument and then the first gives the two second-difference identities stated on the card. They preserve the order of every direction matrix.
Expanding f(A+tG+sH) to mixed order ts gives contributions from G then H and H then G. Thus the Hessian is their sum; a single order equals half the Hessian only for equal directions.
For f(z)=z^2, G=[[0,1],[0,0]], H=[[0,0],[1,0]], the ordered block equals GH=diag(1,0), whereas half the Hessian is I/2. This is an exact counterexample to the printed general identification.
prerequisites: Matrix polynomial evaluation and triangular block inversion
Fréchet derivative of inversion on invertible matrices and product rule
Open invertibility domain for Q(A); no normality or Hermitian functional calculus on blocks
endpoints: Constant and linear polynomials have zero second difference.
Scalar direction matrices commute, so the familiar half-Hessian formula is recovered.
Potential cancellations in P/Q are avoided by stating invertibility of the chosen denominator evaluation.

matrix.scope: Full short proof read; contour mechanism checked, analytic-surface prerequisites remain
steps: Diagonalize the direction B and first approximate it by a matrix with distinct eigenvalues. The characteristic polynomial of A-zB defines eigenvalue branches lambda_j(z)=-b_j z+a_jj+O(1/z) near infinity.

The candidate measure consists of atoms exp(a_jj) at b_j and a density w(s)=(2 pi i)^-1 sum_{b_j<s} integral_C exp(lambda_j(z)+s z) dz. Summing all branches is the entire function Tr exp(A-zB), so w is zero outside [b_min,b_max].

Interchange the finite contour integrals with s-integrals over adjacent eigenvalue intervals. Cauchy's formula gives Tr exp(A-tB) minus the atomic contribution; this verifies the proposed Laplace transform.

On the algebraic surface set g=lambda+s z. Deform onto boundary arcs where Im g=0. Conjugate arcs combine to pi^-1 integral exp(Re g) d(Im z); integration by parts gives minus pi^-1 integral Im z d exp(Re g), with the sign controlled by boundary orientation and the Cauchy–Riemann equations.

Nonnegative mass follows; entirely atomic/reducible cases allow zero density. Mass is Tr exp A. Weak compactness under approximation handles repeated eigenvalues. Shifting B by a scalar and then reflecting its measure gives H of either sign. Bounded support extends the identity to all real t and permits arbitrary derivatives.
prerequisites: Rellich analytic eigenvalue branches for a Hermitian pencil
Algebraic Riemann surfaces, contour deformation and piecewise-smooth level-set boundary regularity
Weak compactness of finite positive measures on a compact interval and uniqueness by moments
endpoints: H=cI gives measure (Tr exp A) delta_c.
H=0 gives a constant F and vanishing positive-order derivatives.
The even-derivative comparison for t>=0 follows by multiplying nonnegative lambda^(2r) by the endpoint bounds on exp(t lambda).

matrix.scope: One-step replacement and finite-sum telescoping reconstructed
steps: For fixed A and a single centered W<=RI, pointwise Taylor gives F_W(1)=F_W(0)+F'_W(0)+integral_0^1(1-t)F''_W(t)dt. Stahl bounds F''_W(t)<=exp(tR)F''_W(0); the expected linear term vanishes.
Second derivatives at zero are homogeneous quadratic functions of W. A Gaussian X with identical real-coordinate covariance therefore has exactly the same expected second derivative.

For Gaussian X, Taylor to order two leaves integral_0^1 (1-t)^2 F'''_X(t)/2 dt. The fourth derivative is nonnegative, so F'''_X(t)>=F'''_X(0). Gaussian symmetry makes E F'''_X(0)=0. This proves the reverse second-order inequality required for comparison.

Apply the one-step inequality after conditioning on every other summand, replacing W_i by an independent matched Gaussian at each stage. The same deterministic shift is retained. Rescaling by theta yields g_R(theta).
prerequisites: Stahl trace-exponential representation
Second- and third-derivative multilinearity at the origin
Gaussian finite exponential moments; conditioning and finite independent-product constructions
endpoints: For R=0, centered negative-semidefinite W must be zero almost surely.
Theta=0 gives equality d=d.
Do not exchange derivatives with expectation on negative t for one-sided unbounded W; integrate pointwise Taylor on [0,1] first.

matrix.scope: Gaussian concentration, scalar bounds and Chernoff optimization reconstructed
steps: Write Z=sum_j g_j A_j. By the Rayleigh formula, lambda_max(Z+Delta) is Lipschitz in g with constant sup_unit_u sqrt(sum_j(u* A_j u)^2)=s_*. Gaussian exponential concentration therefore gives a centered scalar MGF bound theta^2 s_*^2/2.
Trace domination and the replacement theorem give log E Tr exp(theta(Y+Delta)) <= log d+E lambda_max(gZ+theta Delta)+g^2 s_*^2/2. Since g>=theta, Weyl bounds the middle term by theta mu+(g-theta)phi.
For x=R theta in [0,3), k!>=2*3^(k-2) bounds the series for g^2 by theta^2/(1-x/3). The identity g-theta=(g^2-theta^2)/(g+theta) then gives g-theta<=R theta^2/(6(1-x/3)).
Obtain the sub-gamma bound log d+theta mu+V theta^2/(2(1-c theta)), c=R/3. For s>0,V>0 choose theta=a/(1+ca), a=sqrt(2s/V). At the threshold sqrt(2Vs)+cs, the exponent is -s.
For expectation use the matrix Laplace bound and the same parameter with s=log d. If log d=0 take theta down to zero instead. Lower-tail use requires the distinct assumption W_i>=-R_-I.
prerequisites: Gaussian Lipschitz exponential concentration, not only a tail estimate with an unspecified constant
Matrix Laplace-transform bounds
Rayleigh variational formula and Weyl eigenvalue inequality
endpoints: V=0 implies the Gaussian quadratic forms are deterministic; full covariance then vanishes and centered summands vanish.
Strict tail handles R=0 and deterministic equality.
For R>0,s>0 a zero-V threshold still lies strictly above the deterministic mean; at s=0 the bound d>=1 is immediate.

matrix.scope: Entrywise proof and independent-resampling realization reconstructed
steps: Conditional regression evaluates E[(X-X')F(X)] as alpha E[(X-mu)F(X)]. Exchangeability changes the same expression into -E[(X-X')F(X')]. Averaging proves the trace identity.
The tensor identity follows by the same swap calculation, or by expanding E[(X-X') tensor (X-X')] and using regression on each tensor factor.
For independent summands, given all original S_i, average over uniform I and its independent replacement to obtain n^-1 sum_i(S_i-ES_i). Conditioning down to X proves regression.

For the Cauchy consumer, form X'' with a second independent replacement at the same index. Given I=i, X'' is independent of S_i-S_i'; its law is the law of X for every i. Therefore this independence survives averaging over I. It would not follow merely from pairwise exchangeability.
prerequisites: Conditional expectation in finite-dimensional real vector spaces
Exchangeability as equality of joint laws under swapping
Square integrability and Cauchy–Schwarz
endpoints: n=1 gives independent copies and the ordinary covariance identity.
F need not be Hermitian: the trace identity may be complex-valued.
The tensor product retains full entry covariance, not only the product E[(X-mu)^2].

matrix.scope: Theorem 8.1 fully reconstructed from audited finite-matrix ingredients
steps: The exchangeable covariance identity and exact block differences decompose discrete IBP into the matched covariance term and two second-difference remainders. Insert the independent third counterpart before subtracting the derivative.

Differentiate u(t)=E tr_d R_zeta(EX+sqrt(t)(X-EX)+sqrt(1-t)(Z-EZ)) on (0,1). The trace derivative cyclically moves the perturbation, leaving h'=R_zeta^2. Gaussian IBP and discrete IBP cancel the covariance terms exactly.
Each remainder has coefficient n sqrt(t)/4. Delta^2(R_zeta^2)(A,B,C)[G,H] is the sum over positive r+s+t=4 of R(A)^r G R(B)^s H R(C)^t, exactly three terms.

Each word has three resampling differences and four resolvent powers. Applying Holder to the normalized trace/probability noncommutative L3 norms gives M3/n times eta^-4, regardless of dependence between the factors.
The two remainders and three words yield |u'(t)| <= 3 sqrt(t)M3/(2 eta^4). Integrate using integral_0^1 sqrt(t)dt=2/3; dominated endpoint convergence follows from ||R||<=1/eta.
For bounded centered summands, |D_i|^3<=2L D_i^2, E D_i^2=2 E(S_i-ES_i)^2, and normalized trace <= spectral norm imply M3<=4L sigma^2.
prerequisites: Ordered block-difference identities, including resolvent powers
Gaussian and exchangeable integration by parts with explicit integrability
Schatten Holder combined with probability Holder; normalized trace
Hermitian resolvent spectral bound
endpoints: The sign of Im zeta is irrelevant because only its absolute value is used.
All-zero fluctuations give exact equality.
Arbitrary deterministic means are preserved.
No claim of operator-norm or Hausdorff spectral universality follows from this transform bound alone.

matrix.scope: Strong NCK induction reconstructed; elementary subgaussian domination supplied
steps: Symmetrize a centered scalar h: Jensen gives E||sum h_i A_i|| <= E||sum (h_i-h_i')A_i||. These differences are independent symmetric variables.

If E exp(h^2/K^2)<=2, then P{|h-h'|>t}<=4 exp(-t^2/(4K^2)). For standard Gaussian g and u>=0, integrate its density on [u,u+1] and its negative counterpart to get P{|g|>u}>=sqrt(2/pi) exp(-(u+1)^2/2)>=sqrt(2/pi)e^-1 exp(-u^2). This dominates 4 exp(-4(1+u)^2). Therefore |h-h'| is stochastically dominated by 4K(1+|g|).

Use independent scalar quantile couplings and Rademacher signs. The expected norm is coordinatewise nondecreasing in the nonnegative magnitudes because it is convex and even in each coordinate. Contraction gives E||sum(h_i-h_i')A_i|| <=4K E||sum epsilon_i(1+|g_i|)A_i||.

Triangle inequality and Jensen over Gaussian magnitudes give E||sum epsilon_i A_i|| <= (E|g|)^-1 E||sum g_i A_i||=sqrt(pi/2) E||sum g_i A_i||. Thus the complete domination constant 4(1+sqrt(pi/2))K is valid. No generic chaining theorem is needed for this linear comparison.

Lift the series to X_q^N=sum A_i tensor (sqrt(q)D_i^N+sqrt(1-q)G_i^N). D_i^N is diagonal with independent standard normals; G_i^N is symmetric Wigner with every independent upper-triangle coordinate of variance 1/N. At q=1 the lift is N copies of X on diagonal blocks; at q=0 it converges to the semicircular matrix-valued model.

Signed-permutation conjugation invariance forces E h(X_q^N) to be its partial normalized trace tensor I. The second Gaussian derivative's factorized contributions cancel because the diagonal covariance and Wigner covariance act identically on such block scalar expectations. Gaussian covariance interpolation introduces only four-coefficient crossing terms.

The variance parameter of each lift is sigma(X). The diagonal lift has v(X_1^N)=v(X). For N>=2 the Wigner coefficient maximum gives v(X_0^N)=sqrt(2/N)v(X); for N=1 its actual value is v(X), still bounded by sqrt(2/N)v(X). For resolvent moments u(q)=E tr|z-X_q^N|^(-2p), count the differentiated terms to get p*binom(2p+3,3)<=4p(p+2)^3/3. Holder bounds the products by E tr|R|^(2p+4). baseline_audit.informal: Volume sampling of at least d rows of a full-column-rank matrix has a binomial determinant normalizer and is realized by deleting rows with probabilities determined by their leverage scores.
hypotheses: $X\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$ has full column rank, $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and $1\le d\le s\le n$
For $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ let $G_S=X_S^*X_S$
Start at $T=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and, while $|T|>s$, delete i with probability $\det G_{T\setminus\{i\}}/((|T|-d)\det G_T)$ on full-rank states
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\sum_{|S|=s}\det G_S={n-d\choose s-d}\det(X^*X)>0$, and the final subset has probability $p_s(S)=\det G_S/[{n-d\choose s-d}\det(X^*X)]$. Each full-rank-state deletion probability equals $(1-x_i^*G_T^{-1}x_i)/(|T|-d)$, is nonnegative, and the probabilities sum to one. Singular states are unreachable with positive probability. Sampling first t rows by this law and then s rows from them gives the same size-s law.
baseline_audit.notes: Proof audit: the determinant lemma yields 1−leverage, and sum of leverage scores is d. Along a positive path the determinant ratios telescope; each terminal S has (n−s)! deletion orders and denominator product (n−d)!/(s−d)!, producing the claimed normalizer and law. A path first entering a singular state has zero transition probability. Alternative normalizer proof: expand det(X_S*X_S) by Cauchy–Binet; each d-row minor is counted choose(n−d,s−d) times. The same telescoping proves composition. When s=n no deletion occurs; when s=d the algorithm stops before the denominator vanishes. Zero rows are allowed and have deletion probability 1/(|T|−d). This row law for s≥d differs from the existing column law for k≤rank. Complex extension is justified by Gram determinants being real nonnegative and the adjoint determinant lemma. The current declaration index already contains NLAlib.det_add_vecMulVec for the determinant update.

baseline_audit.informal: Sampling rows by their Gram determinant removes the bias of the subsampled least-squares inverse, for every fixed right-hand side.
hypotheses: $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
$X\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$ is full column rank, $1\le d\le s\le n$, and S follows the size-s row-volume law
$D_S$ is the n-by-n diagonal selector and $M_S=(D_SX)^+$ is the d-by-n padded pseudoinverse
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\mathbb E M_S=X^+$. Consequently, for every fixed right-hand-side matrix Y, $\mathbb E[M_SY]=X^+Y$ and $\mathbb E[XM_S]=XX^+$. No general-position assumption is required.
baseline_audit.notes: Proof audit: differentiate Σ_|S|=s det(X*D_S X)=c det(X*X) in an arbitrary matrix direction, with c=choose(n−d,s−d). At a nonsingular subset the derivative identifies 2 Re tr(det(G_S) G_S^−1 X*D_S H). At a singular subset adj(G_S)X*D_S=0, so its derivative is zero, including rank d−1. Equating coefficients gives Σ det(G_S)M_S=c det(X*X)X^+, then divide by the positive normalizer. This derivative proof avoids multiplying undefined inverse updates by zero deletion probabilities. Complex inputs use real directional derivatives and the nondegenerate real Frobenius pairing. s=n gives a deterministic identity, and consistent right-hand sides are recovered exactly on every supported subset.

baseline_audit.informal: The inverse Gram matrix of a determinant-weighted row subset has an explicit Loewner upper bound, with equality exactly under an appropriate support hypothesis.
hypotheses: $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
$X\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$ is full column rank, $1\le d\le s\le n$, and S follows the size-s row-volume law
$G=X^*X$, $M_S=(D_SX)^+$; all inverses are evaluated on supported full-rank subsets
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\mathbb E(G_S^{-1})\preceq\frac{n-d+1}{s-d+1}G^{-1}$ and $\mathbb E[(M_S-X^+)(M_S-X^+)^*]\preceq\frac{n-s}{s-d+1}G^{-1}$. Both are equalities if every size-s row submatrix has full column rank. In particular $\mathbb E\|M_S\|_F^2\le\frac{n-d+1}{s-d+1}\|X^+\|_F^2$, with equality under the same hypothesis.
baseline_audit.notes: Proof audit: on a full-support deletion step, Sherman–Morrison yields Σ_i(1−h_i)(G_T−x_ix_i*)^−1=(|T|−d+1)G_T^−1. Scale by |T|−d+1 and telescope expectations. Without full support, excluded h_i=1 terms remove PSD contributions, producing ≤. Equivalently, the cofactor Cauchy–Binet sum is Σ_|S|=s adj(G_S)=choose(n−d+1,s−d+1)adj(G); singular subsets contribute PSD adjugates but have probability zero. Divide by the normalizer and subtract X^+(X^+)* using unbiasedness for the covariance formula. Requiring full support only at the selected size s is sufficient; general position at size d is stronger than needed. A zero row shows equality can fail. At s=n the covariance is exactly zero.

baseline_audit.informal: Selecting exactly d determinant-weighted rows gives a factor d+1 residual guarantee for fixed least-squares data; the exact expectation needs general position.
hypotheses: $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
$X\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$ has full column rank, $1\le d\le n$, and $Y\in\mathbb K^{n\times p}$ is deterministic
S follows the size-d row-volume law and $\widehat W=X_S^{-1}Y_S$ on its support
$W_*=X^+Y$ and $P_X=XX^+$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\mathbb E\|X\widehat W-Y\|_F^2\le(d+1)\|(I-P_X)Y\|_F^2$, with equality if every d-row submatrix of X is nonsingular. Equivalently, for $H_S=X(D_SX)^+$, $\mathbb E[(I-H_S)^*(I-H_S)]\preceq(d+1)(I-P_X)$, with equality under general position.

baseline_audit.informal: Randomly pivoting an orthonormal basis provides an actual sampling algorithm for a projection DPP and a row interpolative approximation with a sharp expected-error bound.
hypotheses: $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
$Q\in\mathbb K^{m\times k}$ has orthonormal columns, $1\le k\le m$, and $A\in\mathbb K^{m\times n}$ is fixed
Start with $M_0=Q^*$. At step t<k select column j with probability $\|(M_t)_{:,j}\|^2/(k-t)$, then set $M_{t+1}=(I-u_ju_j^*/\|u_j\|^2)M_t$ for $u_j=(M_t)_{:,j}$
S is the unordered set of the k selected pivots
baseline_audit.conclusion: The process is defined almost surely, selects distinct indices, and $\mathbb P\{S=T\}=|\det Q_T|^2=\det((QQ^*)_{T,T})$. Thus $Q_S$ is nonsingular almost surely. For $\widehat A=QQ_S^{-1}A_S$, $\mathbb E\widehat A=QQ^*A$ and $\mathbb E\|A-\widehat A\|_F^2\le(k+1)\|(I-QQ^*)A\|_F^2$, with equality if every k-row submatrix of Q is nonsingular.
baseline_audit.notes: Independent realization proof: write M_t=(I−Π_t)Q* where Π_t projects onto the t selected columns of Q*. Because Q*Q=I_k, M_tM_t*=I−Π_t has trace k−t, so the displayed probabilities normalize and a positive pivot raises rank by one. Gram–Schmidt determinant multiplication gives the ordered path probability |det Q_S|²/k!; all k! orders of a nonsingular S are supported, giving the projection-DPP law. Apply the audited row-volume expectation/risk formulas columnwise. Zero leverage rows are never selected. The source states unconditional equality in its regression and interpolation formulas; the counterexample Q=[1;0], A=[0;1] disproves that. The inequality here is valid for every orthonormal Q; general position restores equality. The greedy pivoting rule on an arbitrary matrix is not claimed to sample its volume law.

baseline_audit.informal: For fixed least-squares data, Gaussian and Haar sketches have exact unbiasedness and residual-error formulas; Haar sketches gain an explicit finite-dimension correction.
hypotheses: $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$; set $\alpha_\mathbb R=1$ and $\alpha_\mathbb C=0$
$A\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$, $B\in\mathbb K^{n\times p}$, $r=\operatorname{rank}A\ge1$, and $r+\alpha_\mathbb K<\ell\le n$
$\Omega\in\mathbb K^{n\times\ell}$ is either iid standard Gaussian or Haar distributed on matrices with orthonormal columns, independently of the fixed data
$\widehat X=(\Omega^*A)^+\Omega^*B$; standard complex Gaussian means $(g_1+ig_2)/\sqrt2$ with independent real standard normals
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\mathbb E\widehat X=A^+B$. Put $L_*=\|(I-AA^+)B\|_F^2$. For Gaussian sketches, $\mathbb E\|B-A\widehat X\|_F^2=(1+r/(\ell-r-\alpha_\mathbb K))L_*$. For Haar sketches the factor is $1+\frac{n-\ell}{n-r}\frac{r}{\ell-r-\alpha_\mathbb K}$. Rank-zero input is the separate exact identity $\widehat X=0$ and residual $\|B\|_F^2$.
baseline_audit.notes: Full local derivation audited: factor A=QR with Q orthonormal and R full row rank; rotate Ω into blocks Ω_1,Ω_2. The solution error is R^+(Ω_1*)^+Ω_2*Q_perp*B, and squared residual is optimum plus ||(Ω_1*)^+Ω_2*Q_perp*B||_F². Gaussian independence plus the inverse-Wishart mean gives r/(ℓ−r−α). For Haar sketches, bottom-block rotational invariance makes the residual covariance scalar; its trace is E tr((Ω_1Ω_1*)^−1)−r. The top Gram has the matrix-Beta representation (W_1+W_2)^−1/2 W_1(W_1+W_2)^−1/2, with independent Wisharts of degrees ℓ and n−ℓ. Cyclic trace and independence give E inverse=[1+(n−ℓ)/(ℓ−r−α)]I. Sign/phase symmetry gives zero mean, with integrability from the finite second moment. This requires a Haar/Stiefel-law and Beta-to-Wishart bridge before formalization. ℓ=n yields exact Haar recovery. No universality extension to sparse/sign sketches is claimed.

baseline_audit.informal: Upper triangular block evaluation gives exact finite differences and derivatives of rational matrix functions, including ordered second differences needed for resolvent comparison.
hypotheses: $A,B,C,G,H\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$; $f=P/Q$ with complex polynomials and $Q(A),Q(B),Q(C)$ invertible

Evaluate $f(M)=P(M)Q(M)^{-1}$ on the full matrix algebra. Define $\Delta f(A,B)[H]$ as the (1,2) block of $f(\begin{smallmatrix}A&H\\0&B\end{smallmatrix})$ and $\Delta^2 f(A,B,C)[G,H]$ as the (1,3) block of $f(\begin{smallmatrix}A&G&0\\0&B&H\\0&0&C\end{smallmatrix})$.
baseline_audit.conclusion: The first difference is linear and the second is bilinear in the direction matrices. baseline_audit.informal: An exchangeable pair with linear conditional regression turns a matrix covariance into a finite difference; independent summand resampling realizes the required pair.
hypotheses: $(X,X')$ is an exchangeable pair of square-integrable Hermitian $d\times d$ matrices, $\mu=\mathbb EX$, and $\alpha>0$ satisfies $\mathbb E[X-X'\mid X]=\alpha(X-\mu)$
$F$ is a measurable matrix-valued function such that $F(X)$ is square-integrable; $\operatorname{tr}$ may be the normalized or ordinary trace, used consistently
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}[(X-\mu)F(X)]=(2\alpha)^{-1}\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}[(X-X')(F(X)-F(X'))]$ and $\mathbb E[(X-\mu)\otimes(X-\mu)]=(2\alpha)^{-1}\mathbb E[(X-X')\otimes(X-X')]$. If $X=\sum_{i=1}^nS_i$ for independent square-integrable summands, $n\ge1$, and $X'=X-S_I+S_I'$ with $I$ independent uniform and $S_i'$ independent copies, these hypotheses hold with $\alpha=1/n$.
baseline_audit.notes: Audit: conditional regression gives alpha times the left side as E tr[(X-X')F(X)]. Swapping the pair changes this to -E tr[(X-X')F(X')]; average the two. Apply the same calculation entrywise to obtain the tensor identity. For independent sums, condition first on all original summands, average the uniform index, then use the tower property; identical distribution of the summands is not required. Square integrability and Cauchy–Schwarz justify every product. The covariance tensor is the bilinear real-coordinate second moment (unstarred tensor product), not the PSD matrix E[(X-mu)^2]; Hermitian symmetry recovers the conjugated entry covariance. The realized pair, not merely an abstract regression hypothesis, is included for use by matrix universality.

$Z$ is Hermitian Gaussian with the same mean and full real-coordinate covariance as $X$

baseline_audit.conclusion: $|G_\zeta(X)-G_\zeta(Z)|\le M_3/\eta^4$. In particular, if $\|S_i-\mathbb ES_i\|_2\le L$ almost surely and $\sigma^2=\|\sum_i\mathbb E(S_i-\mathbb ES_i)^2\|_2$, then $|G_\zeta(X)-G_\zeta(Z)|\le4L\sigma^2/\eta^4$.
baseline_audit.notes: Audit: construct a triple by resampling the same uniform index with two independent copies. The third counterpart is independent of the first pair's difference, which produces the covariance term in discrete IBP. In interpolation EX+sqrt(t)(X-EX)+sqrt(1-t)(Z-EZ), exact matching cancels the Gaussian derivative term and leaves two ordered second differences of h'=R_zeta^2, each with factor n*sqrt(t)/4. Each second difference has three resolvent words with four total resolvent factors and three resampling differences. Resolvent norms are <=1/eta; Schatten/expectation Hölder with exponents 3,3,3 bounds each word by (M3/n)/eta^4. Thus |u'(t)|<=(3/2)sqrt(t)*M3/eta^4 and integration gives exactly M3/eta^4. The bounded case follows from |S_i-S_i'|^3 <=2L(S_i-S_i')^2 and E(S_i-S_i')^2=2E(S_i-ES_i)^2. This proof uses ordered differences and is unaffected by the source's incorrect identification with half a mixed Hessian. All expectations and endpoint limits are justified by finite third moments and the uniform resolvent bound; the source's generic rational IBP statement would need additional integrability for polynomial functions.

baseline_audit.informal: A decoupled subgaussian matrix chaos admits a dimension-free leading variance term, with logarithmic loss confined to coefficient flattenings that place both matrix indices on one side.
hypotheses: $q,m,d_1,d_2\ge1$, $d=\max(d_1,d_2)$, and $A_{i_1,\ldots,i_q}\in\mathbb R^{d_1\times d_2}$
$Y=\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_q}\prod_{j=1}^q h^{(j)}_{i_j}A_{i_1,\ldots,i_q}$, where all coordinates are independent copies of centered real $h$ and $\mathbb E e^{h^2/K^2}\le2$ for $K>0$
$\sigma(A)=\max_{R\subseteq[q]}\|A_{[\,R\cup\{q+1\}\mid([q]\setminus R)\cup\{q+2\}\,]}\|_2$, using coefficient-tensor flattenings
$v(A)=\max_{\varnothing\ne R\subseteq[q]}\|A_{[\,R\mid([q]\setminus R)\cup\{q+1,q+2\}\,]}\|_2$
baseline_audit.conclusion: For each integer $q\ge1$ there exists $C_q>0$, depending only on q, such that $\mathbb E\|Y\|_2\le C_q K^q\{\sigma(A)+[\log(d+m)]^{(q+2)/2}v(A)\}$ for every admissible coefficient family and coordinate law.
baseline_audit.notes: Audit: the linear Gaussian bound follows by Hermitian dilation from the covariance-sensitive Gaussian norm theorem, then Young's inequality moves sqrt(sigma*v)*log(D)^(3/4) into sigma+v*log(D)^(3/2). A direct symmetrization/contraction proof supplies Gaussian domination for arbitrary centered subgaussian coefficients; details are recorded in the derivation audit. For the q-step induction, condition on q-1 coordinate groups. The two variance flattenings are bounded by the strong induction hypothesis, whereas the covariance flattening is bounded by ordinary iterated NCK of degree q-1. Every variance term is a sigma-type flattening; every logarithmic term is v-type. The largest dimensions of these intermediate matrices are at most dm and max(d^2,m), and 3/2+(q-1)/2=(q+2)/2 gives the final exponent. Use log(2D) in the linear step or handle D=1 separately; log(d+m) is positive for all stated dimensions. The nonempty row subset in v is essential. q=1 recovers the full entry-covariance term; coefficients that vanish give both parameters zero. No independence within the original undecoupled chaos is silently assumed: this card is expressly for the decoupled model.
